title: Two clocks
body: Greek myths have an order — first Chaos, then Earth, then the Titans, then Zeus — but no dates. History has dates but not myths. MYTHOS keeps them on two separate tracks: the glowing mythic sequence above, and a dated historical axis below.
takeaway: Myth tells you 'before' and 'after'. History tells you 'when'.

title: In the beginning: Chaos
body: Hesiod's Theogony begins with Chaos — not disorder, but a gaping void. Read Chaos' panel, then switch the reading level to see how scholars discuss the word.
takeaway: Ancient words can mean something different from their modern English descendants.

title: The succession of kings
body: Uranus is overthrown by his son Cronus; Cronus is overthrown by his son Zeus. Follow the sequence through the Age of Titans and the Titanomachy.
takeaway: The Theogony is a story about how Zeus' rule came to be — and why it lasts.

title: One big, quarrelsome family
body: Open the family tree and find Zeus. Gold lines are parent links, pink are partners, red are conflicts. Use 'Isolate branch' to see just his family.
takeaway: Most Greek gods are related, and family conflict drives many myths.

title: When the sources disagree
body: Hesiod says Aphrodite was born from the sea-foam around Uranus; Homer says she is the daughter of Zeus and Dione. Toggle the sources on and off to watch her parents change.
takeaway: There is no single 'correct' Greek mythology — only accounts from different authors.

title: First written down
body: Click a dashed bridge line. Zeus's name appears on clay tablets from the palace at Pylos, long before Homer. That tells us when people worshipped a god called Zeus — not when the myths 'happened'.
takeaway: An attestation is when a tradition is first recorded, not when its story took place.

title: Troy: where myth meets archaeology
body: Hisarlik in Türkiye was a real Bronze Age city that burned. Greeks called it Ilion. But archaeology cannot confirm Achilles, Helen or a ten-year siege. Troy appears on both tracks, treated differently on each.
takeaway: A real place does not make a story historical.

title: Mapping a voyage that isn't on the map
body: Play Odysseus' return. Each leg is coloured by how certain its location is. After Cape Malea the poem leaves the known world — some stops have only proposed sites, and some exist only on the symbolic map.
takeaway: Uncertainty is part of the evidence. MYTHOS shows it instead of hiding it.
